title: The sweetpotato whitefly Bemisia tabaci avoids caterpillar traces to reduce incidental intraguild predation
content:
Abstract
Intraguild predation (IGP) occurs when species competing for shared resources prey upon one another, strongly influencing the population dynamics of those species. While avoidance of IGP by carnivores has been studied well, little is known about how small herbivores avoid incidental IGP by large herbivores. The sweetpotato whitefly Bemisia tabaci (Hemiptera: Aleyrodidae) is a phloem-feeding insect whose eggs and nymphs attached to plant surfaces are immobile. We observed that the polyphagous caterpillar Spodoptera litura (Lepidoptera, Noctuidae) consumed all whitefly eggs and nymphs along with its host plant leaves. To investigate whether the mobile stages of B. tabaci (first-instar nymphs and ovipositing females) address this incidental IGP risks, we conducted experiments in which whiteflies were allowed to choose between leaves with caterpillar traces and leaves without them. The first-instar nymphs did not avoid settling on leaves bearing caterpillar traces, likely due to their limited mobility. In contrast, adult females preferred ovipositing on leaves without caterpillar traces, suggesting a strategy to protect offspring from incidental IGP. The results provide the first evidence that herbivorous insects avoid traces left by larger herbivores, a mechanism previously reported only in small mites. From an applied perspective, identifying the substances responsible for this avoidance could enable environmentally friendly control strategies that manipulate whitefly oviposition behavior to suppress their populations.
